items.stem: An insurer processes several thousand claim forms a day through the same five steps: extract fields, validate against the policy record, check documents, assign severity, and route. The steps never vary and each has a clear success test. Which pattern best fits this workload?
items.principle: determinism before autonomy: use a workflow when the path is known

options.text: A single agent with a tool per step, choosing its own order
options.rationale: Agents are right for open-ended work, but here the model pays planning tokens to rediscover a sequence you already know, and adds run-to-run variation to a process whose whole value is that it never varies.

options.text: An orchestrator agent delegating each step to a subagent
options.rationale: Legitimate when subtasks are independent and context-heavy. This pipeline is strictly linear, so the coordination overhead buys neither parallelism nor independent search.

options.text: A fixed workflow chaining the five steps, one model call each
options.rationale: The path is known and each stage is independently checkable, so a workflow buys determinism, per-stage retries and cheap failure localisation at no loss of capability.

options.text: One call carrying all five instructions and the policy record
options.rationale: Minimises round trips, which is a real advantage. But collapsing five checkable stages into one means a failure anywhere invalidates everything and cannot be retried alone.

items.stem: A security team triages alerts where some need one log query and others need several rounds of narrowing before an analyst can judge them. The team has tried and failed to enumerate the steps up front. Which approach best fits this work?
items.principle: agentic when the path cannot be enumerated in advance

options.text: An agent with a bounded tool set and an explicit step budget
options.rationale: When the number and order of steps genuinely cannot be known before the work starts, delegating control flow to the model is what the agentic pattern is for; the budget and bounded tools are what keep it safe.

options.text: A workflow that branches on the alert type and severity
options.rationale: Branching workflows are right whenever the branch set is knowable. The team has already established that investigations vary in depth within a single alert type, so the branch set does not exist to be written.

options.text: A single prompt preloaded with the recent window of logs
options.rationale: Grounding the model in the logs is sound and often sufficient. It does not address the actual difficulty, which is that each step's result determines what to look at next.

options.text: A prompt chain with a fixed sequence of narrowing steps
options.rationale: Chaining beats one prompt and adds per-step checks. It fixes the depth of the investigation at design time, which is the one thing this workload will not hold still for.

items.stem: A team split a strictly sequential document-review assistant into four agents that hand text to one another. Latency roughly tripled and outputs became less consistent. What best explains the regression?
items.principle: multi-agent earns its coordination cost through parallelism or independent search

options.text: The agents lack a shared memory store across the handoffs
options.rationale: Shared state genuinely fixes context lost at handoffs and would help the consistency symptom. It leaves the tripled latency unexplained and keeps four agents where the work needs one.

options.text: Handoff cost buys no parallelism in a strictly linear pipeline
options.rationale: This names the structural mistake. Multi-agent pays for itself when subtasks run concurrently or need separate context; a linear chain has neither property, so every handoff is overhead and every boundary a place to drift.

options.text: The summarising agent needs a more capable model behind it
options.rationale: Upgrading the weakest stage is a standard and often effective move. It does not account for a regression that began with the split rather than with the model.

options.text: The agents need stricter output schemas at each boundary
options.rationale: Schemas at handoff boundaries are good practice and would cut the inconsistency. They treat the symptom: the boundaries themselves are what should not exist here.

items.stem: A research tool gathers evidence on a company from filings, news, and job postings, then writes one brief. The three gathering tasks share no state and each takes many tool calls. Which orchestration best fits?
items.principle: parallel subagents when subtasks are independent and context-heavy

options.text: A single agent looping through the three sources in turn
options.rationale: Simpler to build and reason about, and correct for lighter work. It serialises three independent jobs and lands all three sources in one context window.

options.text: A fixed workflow with three sequential retrieval stages
options.rationale: The stage boundaries are right and worth keeping. Making them sequential still forfeits parallelism that is available here for free.

options.text: Three parallel subagents each drafting their own section
options.rationale: Parallelises the expensive part, which is most of the win. But nothing ever sees all the evidence at once, so the brief becomes three stapled fragments rather than a synthesis.

options.text: Three parallel gatherers into separate contexts, then a writer
options.rationale: The subtasks are independent and each accumulates heavy context, which is exactly the shape multi-agent is for: concurrency on gathering, and three contexts kept apart so none crowds the others out.

items.stem: A COO says the support team is drowning and wants AI to fix it. Discovery finds agents spend most of each ticket looking up account state across four systems, and little of it composing the reply. Which framing best translates this?
items.principle: solve the measured bottleneck, not the stated symptom

options.text: Deflect a share of incoming tickets with a customer assistant
options.rationale: Deflection is often the highest-leverage support intervention and directly addresses volume. The evidence points at cost per ticket rather than ticket count, so this bets against the discovery data.

options.text: Assemble an account summary before the agent opens the ticket
options.rationale: Discovery located the cost in lookup, not composition, so this is the one option aimed at the measured bottleneck. Translating a business complaint means replacing the stated symptom with the observed constraint.

options.text: Generate suggested replies for support agents to edit and send
options.rationale: A well-proven support pattern with a clear adoption path. It automates the part of the job the team was already fast at.

options.text: Summarise ticket history so agent handoffs lose less context
options.rationale: Real value, and it touches the same underlying problem of assembling context. It is a narrower slice of it, and handoffs were not what discovery flagged.

items.stem: An agent would draft engineering design docs that today cost a senior engineer two afternoons. Reviewers say current quality is fine, and nothing ties these docs to revenue or to any compliance obligation. Which value claim is best supported?
items.principle: claim the value pillar the evidence actually supports

options.text: Productivity: senior hours reclaimed on an adequate-quality task
options.rationale: The only pillar the evidence reaches. Time spent is measured, quality is stipulated as adequate, and nothing else is established, so this is the claim that survives a CFO asking what it rests on.

options.text: Revenue growth, since faster design docs mean faster shipping
options.rationale: Plausible, and the kind of case that does get made. The chain from draft time to shipped revenue has several unmeasured links, and asserting it invites a challenge the team cannot answer.

options.text: Risk reduction through more consistent internal documentation
options.rationale: A sound pillar for documentation work generally. Reviewers have already said quality is fine, so there is no risk delta in evidence to reduce.

options.text: Cost avoidance by reducing the number of senior engineers needed
options.rationale: A legitimate pillar, and the hours are real. Reclaimed hours are not removed headcount, and claiming so tends to cost the project its sponsors.

items.stem: A pipeline retrieves similar past tickets, drafts a reply, and routes it to a human approver. After a quarter, approvers rewrite more of each draft while the corpus and prompt are unchanged. What is the most significant gap here?
items.principle: input to processing to output to feedback: a loop with no feedback cannot improve

options.text: Retrieved tickets are not cached between similar requests
options.rationale: A real and easy optimisation that would cut cost and latency. Neither is the reported problem, and caching would if anything entrench the stale corpus.

options.text: Drafts carry no confidence score to route uncertain cases
options.rationale: Confidence routing is a strong addition to a human-in-the-loop design and would focus reviewer attention. The reviewers' corrections would still go nowhere.

options.text: No path carries approver edits back into the corpus or prompt
options.rationale: The edits are a graded signal the system produces daily and discards. Without a feedback leg it cannot improve, and a static system in a drifting world decays exactly the way the approvers describe.

options.text: There is no fallback when retrieval returns nothing useful
options.rationale: A genuine robustness gap worth closing before it bites. It explains occasional bad drafts, not a steady quarter-long decline.

items.stem: A team has specified input validation, model processing, and output formatting for an invoice assistant, and is about to build. They expect to operate and improve it for years. Which two additions best serve that?
items.principle: a stage is operable only if observable, improvable only if outcomes are captured

options.text: A more capable model behind the processing stage
options.rationale: May well raise quality and is reasonable to try. It improves output without making the system any easier to operate or reason about later.

options.text: Per-stage structured logging tied by a correlation id
options.rationale: Makes the pipeline debuggable as a pipeline rather than three opaque boxes; without it, localising a failure to a stage is guesswork once the system is under load.

options.text: A second formatting pass to enforce style consistency
options.rationale: Addresses a real class of output defect. It is another processing stage, so it adds to what must be operated rather than to the ability to operate it.

options.text: A feedback step recording corrections made downstream
options.rationale: Closes the loop. Without captured outcomes there is no eval set, no drift signal, and no principled basis for any future change to the prompt or the model.

options.text: A larger set of few-shot examples in the prompt
options.rationale: Often the cheapest accuracy win available and worth doing. It is a tuning change to one stage, not a structural property of the architecture.

items.stem: One call asks the model to parse an invoice, match line items against a purchase order, flag discrepancies, and write a summary. Failures are almost always in the matching, but the whole call is retried. Which decomposition best improves reliability?
items.principle: decompose at the boundaries where an intermediate output can be verified

options.text: Split into stages with a checkable output at each boundary
options.rationale: The right seam is wherever you can assert something about the intermediate result. Cutting there shrinks the retry to the failing stage and turns a vague failure into a specific, testable claim about matching.

options.text: Split by source: invoice parsing and purchase-order lookup
options.rationale: A natural decomposition and better than one call. It cuts across the problem: matching spans both sources, so the failing step stays monolithic and unverifiable.

options.text: Keep one call but prompt the model to reason step by step
options.rationale: A reasonable first response to a reasoning failure that may raise the matching rate. The blast radius is unchanged, so failures stay expensive and undiagnosable.

options.text: Keep one call and validate the final summary before sending
options.rationale: End-of-pipeline validation is worth having and would catch bad output. Detecting the failure afterwards still forces a retry of all four tasks to fix one.

items.stem: A policy team answers one-off staff questions about a handbook revised monthly, and each answer must cite the section it came from. No question requires acting on the answer. Which pattern best fits?
items.principle: augmented LLM when a single grounded call answers the question

options.text: An agent with a handbook search tool and a step budget
options.rationale: Genuinely more flexible, and the obvious choice if follow-up questions were in scope. For a self-contained single-hop lookup the autonomy adds latency and variance and buys nothing.

options.text: A workflow of classify, retrieve, answer, then verify
options.rationale: Each stage is defensible and verification is attractive given the citation requirement. It is four calls where one grounded call already produces a citable answer.

options.text: A single augmented LLM call with retrieval over the handbook
options.rationale: One retrieval hop supplies everything the answer needs, citation included. The augmented LLM is the least machinery that fully solves the problem, which is what makes it right rather than merely adequate.

options.text: Place the entire handbook in the prompt for every question
options.rationale: Simple, and it removes retrieval as a source of error, which is a real advantage. It pays for the whole handbook every time and gives no signal about which section the answer came from.

items.stem: A product lead asks for an assistant that understands the roadmap. Pressed on what decision it would change, they describe engineers repeatedly asking which quarter a feature is committed to. Which framing best translates this request?
items.principle: scope to the decision the user actually needs to make

options.text: Build a roadmap assistant that answers open questions on strategy
options.rationale: The literal reading of the request, and the most impressive demo. It is unbounded, has no success test, and nothing in the discovery suggests strategy questions are what anyone is actually stuck on.

options.text: Summarise the roadmap into a digest published to the team weekly
options.rationale: Cheap, useful, and genuinely reduces repeated reading. A digest is stale the moment a commitment moves, which is exactly the question being asked.

options.text: Generate roadmap updates automatically from the issue tracker state
options.rationale: Attacks a real upstream problem: the roadmap drifting from reality. It is a different and larger project than answering the question the engineers keep asking.

options.text: Answer commitment-date questions, grounded in the roadmap of record
options.rationale: Names the decision being made, the evidence it rests on, and a success test you can write down. A vague request becomes solvable only once it is reduced to the question someone is actually asking.
